rows.gloss: in the glorious line of heroes

items.question: What role does a pure mind focused on the guru play in liberation or attainment?
premises: Expansion of awareness occurs in the glorious line of heroes.
A pure mind may be directed toward the guru.
Liberation and attainment are presented as alternative aims.
items.inference: Through expansion of awareness in the heroic lineage, a pure mind directed toward the guru serves as the basis for either liberation or attainment.
uncertainties: The exact nuance of śrīmadvīrāvalīpade as a place, state, or tradition is context-dependent.
items.plain_english: Through the expansion of awareness in the glorious line of heroes, a pure mind directed toward the guru becomes the cause for either liberation or attainment.

rows.gloss: is the cause in both cases also
whatever is pleasing to the mind
but from completeness joined to the life of necessity

items.question: Why can whatever is pleasing and fit for worship serve as a cause in both liberation and attainment?
premises: The same cause can operate in both liberation and attainment.
Whatever is pleasing to the mind and fit for worship may be chosen.
Its effectiveness depends on completeness joined with the force of necessity.
items.inference: Although the chosen object may vary, its causal power in both aims comes from the completeness of conditions grounded in necessity.
uncertainties: The compressed compound niyatiprāṇatāyogātsāmagrītastu allows more than one syntactic unpacking.
items.plain_english: In both liberation and attainment, whatever is pleasing to the mind and fit for worship can be the cause, because its effectiveness comes from the completeness of conditions operating through necessity.

rows.gloss: one whose heart has become pure

items.question: How does a person with a purified heart determine what is truly best among possible attainments?
premises: Attainments and purity of being are both possible outcomes.
A practitioner may have a heart that has become pure.
Such a practitioner reflects on what is highest in that context.
items.inference: Even when attainments are available, the one with a purified heart discerns and reflects upon what is best of all.
uncertainties: The referent of tatra is not explicit within this verse alone.
items.plain_english: Although attainments and purity of being may both arise, a person whose heart has become pure reflects on whatever is best of all in that situation.

items.question: What makes a chosen spiritual goal become truly fruitful according to the cited teaching?
premises: A goal becomes fruitful when pursued with firmness.
The Sāraśāstra is cited as authority.
The one free of conceptual construction succeeds.
items.inference: Firmness makes the goal fruitful, and scriptural authority supports this by stating that success belongs to the one free of conceptual construction.
uncertainties: The exact identity of śrīsāraśāstra is not specified in this verse.
items.plain_english: What one seeks becomes fruitful through firmness, and the Sāraśāstra says that the one who is free of conceptual construction truly succeeds.

rows.gloss: even when what is prescribed by ritual is done

items.question: Why do conceptually divided practitioners struggle even when ritual prescriptions are followed?
premises: Those with conceptual construction struggle even when prescribed rites are performed.
Mantras draw upon a power that must be accessed.
The arising of that power is presented as clear and direct.
items.inference: Ritual performance alone does not remove struggle for the conceptually divided, because effective mantra power depends on directly accessing that underlying force.
uncertainties: The antecedent of tad in tadākramya could refer to a state, method, or support mentioned earlier.
items.plain_english: Those who remain caught in conceptual construction struggle even when they perform what the ritual prescribes, but when that underlying power is truly accessed, the mantras rise clearly and effectively.

rows.gloss: by sayings of the Spanda, this very point

items.question: What do the Spanda teachings establish about practice aimed at attainment or liberation?
premises: Sayings of the Spanda and similar statements explain the same point.
Attainment and liberation are both valid aims.
Worship, recitation, and absorption are the relevant practices.
items.inference: The Spanda teachings confirm that the same principle applies in worship, recitation, and absorption whether the aim is attainment or liberation.
uncertainties: The exact Spanda passages referred to by ityādibhiḥ are not named here.
items.plain_english: Statements from the Spanda and others make this same point clear: in worship, recitation, and absorption, the same principle holds whether one seeks attainment or liberation.

items.question: Where should a purified practitioner establish worship when the heart comes to rest?
premises: A place becomes fit for worship where the heart rests beautifully.
The practitioner is described as pure in being.
The practitioner may still be situated outwardly.
items.inference: The proper place for worship is wherever the heart finds repose, and a purified practitioner may take that as the basis even while acting outwardly.
uncertainties: It is slightly ambiguous whether tatsthānaṃ refers to an inner locus, an outer site, or both.
items.plain_english: Wherever the heart comes to rest in a beautiful stillness, that place is fit for worship; having reached it, a purified practitioner may remain outwardly engaged while grounded there.

rows.gloss: one should perform for the establishment of outer worship

items.question: How should the practitioner perform nyāsa to establish outer worship?
premises: Nyāsa is performed for the establishment of outer worship.
The Mātṛkā and Mālinī are available systems.
They may be used singly or together, in sequence or non-sequence.
items.inference: To establish outer worship, one should perform a general nyāsa using Mātṛkā, Mālinī, or both, following either sequential or non-sequential order.
uncertainties: The practical distinction between krama and akrama here depends on ritual context not fully stated in the verse.
items.plain_english: For the establishment of outer worship, one should perform a general nyāsa using the Mātṛkā, the Mālinī, or both, either in sequence or in non-sequence.

rows.gloss: with the two modes of emission and withdrawal
placed on eyes, ears, nose, cheeks, teeth, and lips

items.question: How are the mantra elements to be placed on the upper parts of the body during nyāsa?
premises: The placement follows the two modes of emission and withdrawal.
The elements are applied individually and in groups.
Specific upper facial locations are named for placement.
items.inference: The nyāsa is performed by applying each element, singly and in pairs, according to emission and withdrawal, across the forehead, face, and other upper facial parts.
uncertainties: The exact mapping of each phoneme to each location is continued in the following verses.
items.plain_english: Using the two modes of emission and withdrawal, one should place the elements one by one and in pairs on the forehead, face, eyes, ears, nose, cheeks, teeth, and lips.

rows.gloss: on shoulder, arm, hand, finger, and nail

items.question: Which phoneme groups and body locations are assigned in this stage of the nyāsa?
premises: Sixteen phonemes ending with visarga are assigned in pairs.
The crown-tuft and tongue are specified locations.
The ka and ca groups are placed on the right and left upper limbs.
items.inference: This stage assigns sixteen phonemes up to visarga in paired placements, including the crown-tuft and tongue, and distributes the ka and ca groups across the right and left shoulders, arms, hands, fingers, and nails.
uncertainties: The exact pairwise mapping of the sixteen phonemes is compressed and partly implicit.
items.plain_english: In this stage, sixteen phonemes ending with visarga are placed in pairs, including on the crown-tuft and tongue, while the ka and ca groups are assigned to the right and left shoulders, arms, hands, fingers, and nails.

rows.gloss: in order on hips, thighs, and so on

items.question: Where should the ṭa, ta, and pa phoneme groups be placed in the continuing nyāsa sequence?
premises: The ṭa and ta groups are to be placed in order on the lower body.
The pa group is assigned to the sides, back, belly, and heart.
A count of nine is specified in this placement.
items.inference: The nyāsa continues by placing the ṭa and ta groups in sequence on the hips and lower limbs, and the pa group across the sides, back, belly, and heart in a ninefold assignment.
uncertainties: The verse compresses the exact distribution that yields the count of nine.
items.plain_english: One should place the ṭa and ta groups in order on the hips, thighs, and so forth, and place the pa group on the sides, back, belly, and heart, making a ninefold assignment.

rows.gloss: led by skin, blood, flesh, sinew, bone, fat, and seed

items.question: How does the text conclude the Mātṛkā nyāsa and introduce the Mālinī nyāsa?
premises: The Mātṛkā nyāsa is associated with bodily constituents beginning with skin and ending with seed.
The verse marks the completion of that exposition.
The Mālinī nyāsa is introduced as the next topic.
items.inference: The text summarizes the Mātṛkā nyāsa as extending through the bodily constituents and then turns to explain the Mālinī nyāsa.
uncertainties: The precise correlation between each constituent and each mantra element is not spelled out in this verse.
items.plain_english: This completes the Mātṛkā nyāsa, extending through the bodily constituents from skin to seed, and now the Mālinī nyāsa is explained.
